 Pentagon Competition Seeks to Build First New Domestic Base in 40 Years 
 DEFENSE DEPARTMENT 
 JUST IN: Pentagon Competition Seeks to Revolutionize Military Bases 
 10/20/2026 
 By 
 Laura Heckmann 
 Defense Dept. photo
 WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Defense Department recently launched an initiative to build a future base that will take into account both rapidly evolving technology as well as  the troops that will use it.
 The Next Great American Base initiative, announced in late September, is a project to build a “premier, world-class power projection platform from the ground up,” according to a department release.
 The new installation will be engineered to operate completely off the commercial grid and will feature independent power generation, autonomous systems and advanced air defenses, according to the release. 
 A memorandum to senior Pentagon leadership on the initiative titled “Next Great American Base Site Selection and Development Process” said the project is the result of rapid advancements in disruptive technologies and persistent and sophisticated cyber intrusions against defense architecture, necessitating a modernized and resilient posture.
 The memo directed Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations and Environment Dale Marks to lead an effort to identify, evaluate, select and prepare an optimal site for the installation and immediately triggered a nationwide competitive site-nomination and evaluation process.
 “We’ve looked at years and years of a lack of investment in our homeland infrastructure, and you see that. These are things that we are trying to fix,” Marks told reporters during a Defense Writers Group event Oct. 20. “It's pretty impossible to try to run a 21st century military on a 20th century foundation.”
 Marks said his goal is to harden the homeland and make it defensible, reiterating a recurring belief in the current administration that the homeland is no longer a sanctuary. The Next Great American Base initiative is part of that effort. 
 “We have not constructed a new military base in this nation in 40 years, and so we are launching a nationwide merit-based competition,” Marks said. “This is not another soulless bureaucratic installation built with enduring classical architecture. It's going to be a world-class dynamic platform for power projection.”
 The Defense Department has reached out to governors, industry, partners and adjutant generals for their “best and brightest ideas,” he said. 
 “Bring us what you think this future looks like.” If chosen, the best idea will be the basis for a self-sustaining shield, he said.
 Underpinning the effort is a program called Fortress America, also announced in September, which Marks called the “pilot or forerunner of what we’re trying to do” and a strategic insurance policy. “It's how we generate power independently, so that you're no longer reliant on the grid.” 
 The Defense Department release said Fortress America “ensures that every major U.S. military installation generates its own independent power so bases remain lit, aircraft fly and command centers stay online even if the civilian grid is taken down by cyberattack or sabotage.”
 The initiative aims to harden every installation on U.S. soil against cyber intrusion, sabotage and drones, the release said.
 When preparing for a project like the Next Great American Base, the hardest part is building something from the ground up, a senior defense official told reporters on background. 
 For example, a request to place two brigade combat teams somewhere in the world would be doable today because “I can tell you how many people, what kind of equipment, how much I need to station, etc., etc., etc.,” the official said. “We're not doing that.”
 Instead they are building from the ground up a foundational capability that allows it to be done “very, very differently,” the official said. The plan examines bases that may host six-generation jet fighters, rockets or ships, “and the challenge here is a little bit different in that as the states bring it to us, we're actually going to match mission to location, as opposed to the other way around.”
 A future base will take into account the future force that is being built — whatever new capabilities and new military occupational specialties the services are investing in, the official said.
 “I need a place that can actually match those capabilities, and do so in a way that takes advantage of autonomy, takes advantage of AI, takes advantage of newer capabilities, and then what happens is, as we build that, then I can take that into Fortress, so that I can take the best of what we have as a future capability,” the official said.
 An ongoing assessment is trying to determine costs. First and foremost is to assess every single installation, roughly 500, and look at what makes sense at those installations, the official said.
 Meanwhile, the official said the Defense Department is using lessons learned in the Middle East to better defend future bases against drone attacks, including meetings with Central Command and conducting assessments from an installation perspective. 
   “Part of this is what will the global posture be in the future, and what does that require us to have? And as we make those investments, making sure that we're doing [so] very strategically about where we need to be,” the official said.
 Bases are a weapon system, not just a piece of real estate, the official said.  
 “In the Middle East, what we've seen is a different posture and a different way in which this was fought, and we've learned a great deal about that,” the official said.  Warfare has changed the way the adversary wants to attack bases and it's “why we're thinking about how the future of basing is going to look in how I defend it.” 
 In addition to taking those lessons learned and trying to apply them, "we're also smarter about it," the official said. "In the past we might have said potentially, ‘Hey, what about those drones?’ Well, those drones are real, and they can cause real damage."

 Re: Pentagon Competition Seeks to Build First New Domestic Base in 40 Years 
 We have concentrated too many of our military bases onto large bases where the military and their families live too isolated from the civilian communities. In the late 50s and early 60s we had Nike bases scattered around Connecticut where there was more interaction with the local communities. In the 70s are German counterparts had active-duty troops stationed in Localized Kasernes and their reinforcing Reserves scattered among adjacent communities. The active-duty troops formed the key structure of the units who were fleshed out by the reserves. We need more integration of our military into the local communities where they could forge a closer partnership with the local populace and reinforcing Reserve and National Guard Units. It would also aid recruitment and training. The advent of robotics and highly intelligent systems lends itself to dispersing rather than concentrating key resources. Dispersing resources would also enhance the chain of commands ability to think more independently and in a timelier fashion which has always been a proven strength of our military. 
 John D Warnock at 12:41 PM
